standard.title: Identify strategies for geographical action
standard.description: identify a strategy for action in relation to environmental, economic, social or other factors, and explain potential impacts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have prior skills proposing actions from F–6 HASS (AC9HS6S06: propose actions or responses to issues or challenges and use criteria to assess the possible effects). This standard extends that to the geographical context — proposing individual and collective action in response to geographical phenomena, explaining potential impacts, and reflecting on how personal values influence explanation of impacts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify a strategy for action in relation to a geographical phenomenon or challenge and explain its potential impacts.

nodes.label: Individual action in response to geographical phenomena
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can propose individual action in response to a geographical phenomenon or challenge, supporting the proposal with geographical reasoning.
nodes.minimum_width: Students propose at least one individual action in response to a geographical challenge and explain why it would be effective.
nodes.typical_width: Students propose individual actions in response to geographical phenomena or challenges — e.g. reducing individual water footprint, choosing active transport for liveability — supporting each proposal with reasons connected to the geographical analysis conducted.
wider: Evaluate the potential impact of scaling individual action — if many individuals took the same action, would it produce meaningful change? What scale of uptake would be needed?
Compare individual action to collective action for the same challenge and evaluate which is better suited to addressing the geographical cause
Examine cases where well-intentioned individual actions have unintended negative impacts — e.g. increased water recycling in one area reducing river flows to downstream users

response_modes.reason: Individual action proposals often lack connection to the geographical analysis. The reasoning scaffold: geographical finding → mechanism connecting individual action to that finding → why this action addresses the identified cause or condition → expected impact.

success_criteria: Proposes at least one individual action in response to a geographical phenomenon or challenge.
Supports the proposal with geographical reasoning that connects the action to the identified problem.

nodes.label: Collective action and geographical change
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can propose collective action in response to a geographical phenomenon or challenge, supporting the proposal with reasons and explaining the geographical mechanism through which it would produce change.
nodes.minimum_width: Students propose at least one collective action and explain how it would address a geographical challenge at a community or policy scale.
nodes.typical_width: Students propose collective actions in response to geographical phenomena — e.g. community water conservation guidelines, planning for sustainable and liveable cities — supporting proposals with reasons including expected geographical impacts and mechanisms of change.
wider: Compare two collective actions at different scales (local vs national) addressing the same geographical challenge — examine what scale of action is needed to address a particular cause
Develop a collective action proposal that involves multiple stakeholders — map the different roles, interests and contributions of each stakeholder group
Examine historical examples of collective action that produced geographical change (e.g. water management reforms, urban greening programs) and evaluate what made them effective

response_modes.reason: Widening to collective actions at different scales — community, municipal, state, national — prevents students from treating all collective action as equivalent and reveals how the scale of the problem determines the appropriate scale of response.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Collective action at different scales is directly connected to the elaborations' examples (community water guidelines, ecopolis planning). Students who can articulate why different scales of collective action address different geographical causes develop sophisticated understanding of the relationship between geographical processes and policy responses.
success_criteria: Proposes at least one collective action and explains how it would address a geographical challenge.
Identifies the scale at which the collective action operates and explains why that scale is appropriate.

nodes.label: Personal values and explanation of potential impacts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can reflect on how personal values and attitudes influence explanations of potential impacts of actions on geographical phenomena.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify at least one way their personal values or experiences influence how they explain a potential impact.
nodes.typical_width: Students reflect on the influence of personal values and attitudes on explanations of potential impacts — e.g. how availability of technology and infrastructure shapes what is perceived as a liveable place; how cultural and economic values lead to different assessments of water use priorities — producing an explanation that is aware of its own value-basis.
wider: Examine the same proposed action from two different value perspectives (e.g. economic development vs environmental conservation) and explain how each perspective produces a different impact assessment
Compare the impact explanation produced by a community directly affected by a geographical challenge with the explanation produced by a policymaker or researcher — examine the sources of difference
Reflect on how geographical positionality (where you live, your cultural background, your economic situation) shapes which impacts are visible and which are invisible

response_modes.reason: Value-awareness in impact explanation requires students to step outside their own perspective and identify its premises. Scaffolding: what values or assumptions underlie my impact explanation? Who might assess impacts differently and why?

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Reflexive awareness of how values shape geographical explanation is a sophisticated intellectual skill that develops geographical literacy beyond factual knowledge. It prepares students for critical engagement with competing claims about geographical challenges throughout the curriculum.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one personal value or attitude that influences their explanation of a potential impact.
Explains how a different value perspective would produce a different assessment of the same impact.

nodes.label: Integration: strategy, impact and values
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students identify a strategy for action in relation to a geographical challenge and explain its potential impacts — integrating individual and collective dimensions and value-awareness.
nodes.minimum_width: Students produce a strategy proposal (individual or collective) and explain at least two potential impacts, noting one value dimension that influences the impact explanation.
nodes.typical_width: Students produce an integrated strategy proposal that: identifies a geographical challenge, proposes individual and/or collective action, explains potential impacts across multiple dimensions, and reflects on how values shape the impact explanation — presented as a coherent, reasoned proposal rather than separate components.
wider: Develop a strategy proposal that includes both individual and collective components, explains potential impacts at multiple scales, and explicitly acknowledges competing values among different stakeholders
Evaluate the strategy using criteria from K08 (effectiveness, feasibility, equity, environmental impact) and revise the proposal based on the evaluation

response_modes.reason: The standard brings together individual action, collective action and value-awareness into a single strategy proposal with impact explanation. Integration practises producing this as a connected geographical argument rather than three separate tasks.

success_criteria: Produces a strategy proposal with at least two potential impacts explained.
Reflects on at least one value dimension that shapes the impact explanation.
